newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian PM's party votes as split looms.
newsitem.headline: Indian PM's party votes as split looms.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's fractious party voted on Thursday to choose a leader in an election overshadowed by corruption allegations and the prospect of a bitter split in its ranks.
Leaders of the Janata Dal, the largest group in Gujral's 15-party United Front coalition, used the ballot box for the first time in the party's nine years to select their leader.
But the dose of democracy, imposed by an activist Election Commission and supported by the Supreme Court, was obscured by the incumbent party leader's call to boycott the polls.
Janata Dal president Laloo Prasad Yadav, who is chief minister of the populous eastern state of Bihar, said voter lists had been rigged against him.
"I will not allow anybody to capture the party through proxy and that is why I have given the call for boycott of the elections," Yadav said on Wednesday.

Yadav's supporters in Bihar said they would hold their own convention on Saturday in the state capital Patna to re-elect him as leader of their faction. Results of the balloting in the main faction were not expected before Sunday.
Yadav and 55 others have been indicted by federal police in a $280-million corruption case involving the alleged embezzlement of state animal husbandry funds.
Last month, the case forced a junior minister to resign from Gujral's two-month-old government. But Yadav, who says he is innocent, has refused to step down either as chief minister or party leader.

Gujral, who with other senior leaders has urged Yadav to quit, played down the split as he cast his vote at party headquarters in Delhi. "There could be differences of opinion and perception, but we all belong to one party," he said.
Former prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda had veiled criticism for Yadav. "Some of the senior leaders want to avoid the election and they tried their best," he said.
Newspapers underscored the tension that had built between Yadav and the main contender, Sharad Yadav, who is also from Bihar but no relative.

"Mr (Laloo) Yadav decided to complain against the constitution of the electoral college only after his efforts to have himself anointed as party chief failed," The Hindu newspaper said in an editorial.
"It is clear that the dispute that is being witnessed in the Janata Dal is merely a feud between two factions."
Sharat Yadav said: "If you wipe out all this dust that has gathered during the past nine years, there is bound to be some problem."
Gujral has tried to keep above the fray for fear of being dragged into a fight that could weaken his grip on power.
Political analysts said Laloo Yadav was not expected to withdraw his crucial support to the centre-left alliance.
But continued tension in the coalition's main party would doubtless complicate Gujral's task and could embolden its make-or-break ally, the Congress party.
